assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal for optical lattice clocks removed the trade-off between many atoms and Doppler/recoil/collisional shifts, and Ye's group turned it into clocks at the 1e-18 level. This is precision atomic physics of the kind I trust: a clean, original idea made quantitative through accurate atomic-structure theory (magic wavelengths, blackbody and higher-order shifts). The clocks now probe relativistic time dilation over millimetres, constrain variation of constants and open a route to redefining the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the decisive conceptual proposal and first demonstrations; Ye's JILA group brought the stability and accuracy to the frontier and the many-body/spin-exchange work. Both names are well supported. Others (for example Hollberg, Hall, Hänsch on the comb side, or ion-clock groups) share credit for the broader field, but the lattice-clock specifically fits two laureates.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others) reproduce and compare clocks, and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good, because the redefinition of the second is approaching.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would regard this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize.
Credit shared with ion-clock and comb communities; I am relying on memory for details of the early lattice-clock priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller's 1995 proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, and their later proposals for atomic quantum simulation (cold atoms in optical lattices, Rydberg gates), supplied the conceptual blueprint that made controlled quantum many-body systems a laboratory reality. It is original, clear and has changed what experimentalists attempt. Fundamentally it shows that quantum states can be engineered and controlled atom by atom.
assessment.attribution: The pair are the natural and almost inseparable credited theorists; the 1995 ion-gate proposal is jointly theirs. Experimental demonstrations (Wineland's group, Blatt's group, and others) are separate credit and Wineland already has the 2012 prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature: ion-trap gates, Rydberg gates and optical-lattice simulators have been realised by many independent groups for two decades, so the theory is thoroughly validated.
uncertainties: A concern that theory-only recognition overlaps with the experimental recognition in 2012; the committee may prefer to pair theory with experiment (see B019).
Exact priority across Cirac-Zoller, Jaksch-Zoller and others is from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising the Hubbard model with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition to fermionic Mott insulators and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, gave an entirely new way to study strongly correlated quantum matter with controllable parameters. It is a genuine discovery platform with clean theory-experiment comparison, which I value.
assessment.attribution: The experimental names Bloch, Esslinger and Greiner carry the decisive demonstrations (Mott transition, fermionic Hubbard physics, quantum gas microscope). The theory contribution of Zoller and Cirac is credited under a separate entry (B046) and I deliberately did not list them here. Five names are credited, so restricting to three involves a choice that excludes Zoller and Cirac.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproduced widely, though ultracold-atom Hubbard simulators have not yet settled the open questions (the doped Hubbard phase diagram) that motivated them. Recognition is timely but the headline scientific payoff is still developing.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit between theory proposals and experiments and among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and other experimentalists is not unique.
Competition for the prize slot with B046 and B020; both could not be easily awarded together.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that phases, not only forces, carry physical content, and that gauge potentials and adiabatic geometry have observable consequences. It is a deep point about quantum mechanics and has been absorbed into atomic, molecular, optical and condensed-matter physics (Berry curvature, topological phases, polarisation, molecular conical intersections).
assessment.attribution: Aharonov-Bohm (1959) was jointly Aharonov and Bohm; Bohm died in 1992, so the prize cannot include him, and Aharonov and Berry are distinct contributions (Aharonov-Anandan generalisation also relevant, Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins as precursors). A shared prize for the geometric-phase idea is defensible but credit is historically tangled.
assessment.maturity: Extremely well confirmed (Chambers 1960, Tonomura electron holography, many Berry-phase experiments). The question is not maturity but whether recognition is now late and whether the committee wishes to honour a conceptual rather than single-discovery contribution.
uncertainties: Priority issues involving deceased or uncredited contributors (Bohm, Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam).
Whether the two contributions are thematically unified enough for one prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms has become a precision tool for measuring gravity, the gravitational constant, rotation, the fine-structure constant and for testing the equivalence principle. It extends the quantum-mechanical wave nature of matter to ever larger objects and tests where quantum meets gravity, which fits my interest in the quantum/classical boundary.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer), Pritchard (first atom interferometers, with Chu and others) and Kasevich (atomic fountain gravimeters, gyroscopes) are strong; Chu already has the 1997 prize and Müller and Chu-related groups complicate credit. A three-person set is workable but the omission of others is a real allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the key principles; precision applications are reproduced by independent groups, though headline fundamental tests (large-momentum-transfer, long-baseline) are still under development.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 prize and with 2001 and 2012 recognitions in atomic physics.
Uncertain which individuals are decisive for the interferometer itself versus its applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol link the foundations of quantum mechanics (no-cloning, Bell inequalities) to secure communication. The idea is original and clear, and it makes an operational use of entanglement that is conceptually in line with the 2022 prize. For me the foundational content is the draw, not the technology.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91) are the clear core and form a natural three-person set; Wiesner's conjugate-coding precursor is not in the credited names and is a priority question, and Wiesner's status is a sensitivity.
assessment.maturity: The protocols are theoretically mature and have been implemented widely (satellite, fibre), but practical security (device imperfections, side channels) is still evolving; the Nobel-worthy idea is stable.
uncertainties: Strong overlap with 2022 and the committee may feel the quantum-information area has been recently covered.
Wiesner's earlier precursor may complicate credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Caves' 1981 proposal that squeezed vacuum can beat the shot-noise limit in interferometers, followed by its realisation in GEO600 and LIGO, shows quantum noise being engineered in the largest precision instrument ever built. It is a fundamental application of quantum optics to the measurement limit, with direct impact on gravitational-wave detection that has itself been honoured in 2017.
assessment.attribution: Caves is the theoretical originator. Squeezed-light generation involved several experimentalists (Slusher, Kimble, Wu, and others) not all in the credited set; Schnabel and Mavalvala are credited for the implementation in detectors. Kimble is credited but was excluded by my choice, which reflects my view that detector implementation is the prize-worthy leap; other members might weigh Kimble's earlier experiments more heavily.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: squeezing is now in routine operation in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, which is independent confirmation. Still, the discovery interpretation is partly technical.
uncertainties: Credit for the first observations of squeezed light is split and not fully captured by the credited names.
Might be viewed as an enabling technique rather than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The three-step recollision model and the Lewenstein strong-field quantum theory explain high harmonics and attosecond pulses and sit underneath attosecond science. This is the field I know best, so I rate its importance highly but declare that closeness. The 2023 prize already recognised the experimental harmonic and attosecond pulses (Agostini, Krausz, L'Huillier) and so a further prize here would be on the strong-field theory and recollision physics.
assessment.attribution: Corkum (semiclassical three-step model, 1993) and Lewenstein (quantum strong-field approximation with L'Huillier and others, 1994) are the central figures; Kulander and Schafer simultaneously developed related ideas, and L'Huillier already is a laureate. A two-person prize is neat but the credit for the recollision picture also involves Kulander.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and independently validated (high harmonic spectroscopy, laser-induced electron diffraction, attosecond pulse generation in many labs). The question is timeliness: a prize for the same research programme only three years after 2023.
uncertainties: Overlap with 2023; I am close to this community (collaborator of a 2023 laureate), so my ranking may be biased.
Kulander and Schafer credit is outside the supplied names.
